newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's King Hussein leaves for Bahrain, Qatar.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's King Hussein leaves for Bahrain, Qatar.

text.p: King Hussein of Jordan left for Bahrain on Tuesday to crown a gradual reconciliation in ties from strains caused by the 1990 Gulf crisis, officials said.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, who has been promoting better ties with the Gulf since he formed his government in February, accompanied the king on his first trip to Manama in over five years, they added.

From Bahrain, King Hussein will go to Qatar on Wednesday -- his second trip to the Gulf state in two years -- to discuss regional developments and find ways to boost growing economic and political ties.

With the exception of Oman, Jordan's traditional ally, Amman angered all its Arab Gulf allies because of its perceived pro-Baghdad support after Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, sparking the Gulf crisis.
But its turn against Baghdad after top Iraqi defections in August 1995 and tough anti-Iraq policies by Kabariti helped Jordan improve ties with most Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia.
Ties with Kuwait, where popular anti-Jordanian sentiments remain strong despite several top meetings between officials from both countries over the past year -- have yet to improve.
Kuwait's minister of Islamic affairs arrived in Amman on Wednesday to attend a meeting with his Arab counterparts, the first ministerial visit to Amman from Kuwait.
Jordanian officials hope the fence mending process will pick up after Kuwaiti parliamentaty elections in October. It is waiting for Kuwait to allow it to reopen its embassy after a six year closure.
King Hussein, facing a growing economic crisis, wants oil-rich Arab Gulf states, once his main bankrollers, to employ more Jordanians after it stopped recruiting them during the Gulf crisis.

Despite the crisis, Jordan has maintained strong security links with most in the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- grouping Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.
Several Jordanian army, police and intelligence officers helped train their GCC counterparts in the last four decades.
